transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-12
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE); Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE); Dr. Priya Nair (Velora Head of ML); Marco Ruiz (Velora CTO); Sofia Turner (Velora PM)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be partial): discuss model choices for long clinical notes, multilingual generation, and tool-calling for patient data lookups.

00:00 Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm maya from Redwood, gonna kick off, sorry if my audio is iffy today, can you hear me ok?
00:06 Marco Ruiz: yeah, we can hear you, good to meet you both.
00:10 Maya Chen: great. quick intros - liam, do you want to say hi?
00:14 Liam O'Connor: hi all, liam o'connor, solutions eng, mostly deep on inference and dedicated ops, i'll handle the performance and deployment details.
00:20 Dr. Priya Nair: priya here, i run the ml team, we're evaluating open model families for our clinical summarization pipeline, main thing is fidelity to medical terms across english/spanish and japanese.
00:31 Sofia Turner: sofia - product, i'll own the acceptance criteria and rollout plan.
00:35 Maya Chen: thanks. quick agenda: model selection, context and tokenization discussion, tool-calling needs, deployment and security. sound good?
00:42 Marco Ruiz: yes. first, can you explain the practical differences between hosted and dedicated? we want to understand where the bottlenecks might be.
00:50 Liam O'Connor: sure. hosted gives you quick API access, we manage models and autoscaling, lower ops burden; dedicated gives you reserved GPU pool for predictable throughput and isolated capacity — lower variance latency and often better for heavy steady workloads. private/vpc means the control plane is separate and you can run in your VPC or on-prem for data residency and extra isolation.
01:08 Dr. Priya Nair: is token-level caching supported across all three? we rely on prefix cache for repeated patient templates.
01:13 Liam O'Connor: yes, caching and KV cache is supported in the runtime across modes, but dedicated/private lets you tune cache sizing and persistence policies more tightly. hosted has smart defaults and shared optimization but you can enable customer-specific caching configs on dedicated.
01:27 Sofia Turner: our note lengths average 18k tokens but some records are whole-visit transcripts that go to ~45k tokens; what's realistic for open models?
01:35 Liam O'Connor: good question. there are two places to consider: model architecture/context window and runtime memory/kv behavior. some models are 32k native, others 64k or beyond. for 45k you either pick a 64k-capable model or shard + intelligent prefix caching/retrieval. we typically recommend 64k models for that distribution, or using retrieval-first to reduce raw token input.
01:56 Dr. Priya Nair: we tested a 13B model and saw hallucinations on complex drug interactions. would a larger parameter model fix that or do we need RLHF/fine-tuning?
02:05 Liam O'Connor: larger models usually improve factuality, but domain-specific fine-tuning or retrieval-augmented generation often gives more predictable gains. also quantization can affect accuracy; 4-bit quantized variants sometimes drift on edge medical terms. we can show benchmark examples.
02:22 Marco Ruiz: which open families do you suggest we try first? we've been told to consider Mistral, Mixtral, Falcon, and Llama-derived models.
02:29 Maya Chen: for your mix of long context + multilingual + clinical accuracy, we typically run parallel benchmarks: (1) 34B-class Mistral variants 64k, (2) Falcon 40B where available, (3) Llama-family (mixtral included) and a tuned 70B if cost allows. Mistral 34k/64k variants have good instruction-following and are cost-effective; Falcon often has strong zero-shot pass in some languages, but multilingual coverage varies.
02:53 Dr. Priya Nair: any gotchas for japanese medical terms — tokenization issues?
03:00 Liam O'Connor: tokenizers differ. some models use SentencePiece variants that break japanese into many pieces, increasing token counts; that affects both cost and prompt fitting. we recommend running your sample set through tokenizers before deciding. we'll do that as part of the benchmark.
03:18 Sofia Turner: tool-calling — we need the model to call an internal service to fetch structured patient labs and also run SQL queries against our analytics DB. how does that work?
03:27 Maya Chen: Redwood supports function/tool calling patterns and structured outputs. runtime can enforce schemas on responses and we have connectors patterns (we can demo a SQL connector). for security, tool calls in Private may use network controls to keep egress within VPC.
03:41 Marco Ruiz: latency for tool calls — we can't have a hundred-millisecond stall per token on queries. what's typical?
03:48 Liam O'Connor: tool-call latency depends on the external service. Redwood streaming helps: you can stream model output and have asynchronous tool invocation to avoid blocking the whole generation. with dedicated capacity and colocated connectors, p99 end-to-end for simple tool-calls can be sub-500ms; complex DB queries will vary.
04:06 Dr. Priya Nair: can i run a small pilot on hosted to validate model selection and then move to dedicated/private for production?
04:12 Maya Chen: absolutely. common path: prototype on hosted, then commit to Dedicated for SLAs and predictable cost, or move to Private if you need tighter controls. we can help port prompt/config and maintain model versions across modes.
04:21 Sofia Turner: compliance — we need SOC2 plus regional data residency in eu for some patients. can Redwood Private satisfy that?
04:27 Maya Chen: yes, Private with customer-managed VPC and our on-prem packages can meet residency requirements; we also provide KMS integration and detailed audit logs. we'll share the security brief with SOC2/ISO artifacts.
04:40 Marco Ruiz: pricing — high-level, is 34B Mistral cheaper than a 70B Llama variant when comparing cost per token?
04:46 Liam O'Connor: often yes — 34B class models are more cost-effective on token/unit economics. larger models have higher GPU cycles per token. our Optimize tool can estimate cost per 1M tokens across quantization profiles and batching.
04:59 Dr. Priya Nair: we need to evaluate 3 axes: clinical accuracy, multilingual fidelity, and cost. can you propose a minimal benchmark matrix?
05:07 Maya Chen: yes — we'll run 1) accuracy tests on a 200-case gold set for drug interactions and diagnoses, 2) multilingual BLEU/ROUGE-like checks on translated summaries, 3) latency and cost for average and tail-case prompt sizes including 45k tokens. we'll include quantized and FP16 runs.
05:27 Marco Ruiz: how about fine-tuning vs instruction-tuning vs retrieval? we prefer not to full-fine-tune a 70B unless necessary.
05:34 Liam O'Connor: retrieval-augmented generation plus light instruction-tuning or LoRA is often the sweet spot: you get domain grounding without training a full model. for critical labels you may want a small fine-tune for calibration.
05:48 Dr. Priya Nair: can you demo tool-calling with a SQL example? we'd like to see schema enforcement.
05:54 Liam O'Connor: we can — liam will run a short SQL tool demo in the follow-up SE deep-dive.
05:59 Maya Chen: ok, let's capture next steps.
06:02 Marco Ruiz: yes.
06:04 Maya Chen: recap: we'll send the benchmark spreadsheet and a proposed 3-model matrix (Mistral 34B 64k, Falcon 40B-ish, Llama-mixtral 70B-lite), include tokenization reports for your sample set, share security brief and SOC2 artifacts, and schedule a 90-minute SE deep-dive with live tool-calling demo.
06:21 Sofia Turner: that works. timelines? suggest we aim to get pilot data in two weeks.
06:27 Maya Chen: we'll target the benchmarks to start next week and deliver initial results 7-10 business days after we get your prompt sets.
06:34 Dr. Priya Nair: i'll send three prompt sets and a 200-case gold set by Monday — thanks.
06:39 Maya Chen: perfect. any other blockers?
06:42 Marco Ruiz: one last Q — are you able to provide on-prem packaging for air-gapped sites?
06:46 Liam O'Connor: yes, we have an on-prem package for regulated deployments; it's a bigger lift but supported. we'll include the outline in the security brief.
06:54 Sofia Turner: thanks everyone, that was helpful.
06:57 Maya Chen: thanks all, we will follow up with the artifacts and book the SE deep-dive.
07:02 Meeting end.
